readerTitle: The nearest country on the map may be the farthest market
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Ghemawat 2001, 무역 중력 모형) + 가상 사례 (가정용품 소매 체인, 철제 선반 제조사)
insight: 시장 사이의 거리는 킬로미터가 아니라 문화, 제도, 지리, 경제라는 네 가지 차이의 합이다.
misconception: 가까운 이웃 나라나 인구가 가장 많은 나라가 첫 해외 시장으로 가장 쉽고 좋다.

sources.text: Ghemawat, P. (2001). Distance Still Matters: The Hard Reality of Global Expansion. Harvard Business Review, September 2001.
국제무역의 중력 모형(gravity model) 연구 전반: 무역량은 경제 규모에 비례하고 거리에 반비례하며, 공통 언어·국경·무역협정이 무역을 늘린다는 결과
소매 체인과 선반 제조사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Ghemawat(2001)이 거리를 문화(Cultural), 제도(Administrative), 지리(Geographic), 경제(Economic)의 네 차원으로 나눈 점을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 프레임워크 이름(CAGE)을 쓰지 않고 원리만 설명했습니다.
5번 카드의 중력 모형 내용은 방향만 서술했고 구체적 배수(예: 공통 언어가 무역을 몇 배 늘린다)는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 Ghemawat(2001)에 인용된 원 연구를 확인한 뒤 넣으세요.
6번 카드의 업종별 민감도 예시(무겁고 싼 제품은 지리, 규제 제품은 제도 등)는 Ghemawat의 논지를 쉽게 풀어 쓴 것입니다. 원문 표현과 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.
모든 사업 사례와 거리·국가 설정은 가상입니다. 특정 국가의 관세나 인증 제도에 대한 사실 주장은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The nearest country on the map may be the farthest market
body: Open a map and draw a circle around your business. The countries inside it look like your easiest next step.

Now picture a truck crossing that border. It meets a new language on every label, a new rulebook for your products, and shoppers who earn half or twice what yours do. The drive is short. The trip is long.

image.label: A map with a short road that turns into a maze at the border
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 지도 위 짧은 도로가 국경을 넘자마자 표지판, 서류 더미, 다른 글자의 라벨로 가득한 미로로 바뀜. 실제 국가명, 국기, 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should your stores go first?
body: You run a chain of 40 home-goods stores. You want to open abroad and have two serious options, plus one tempting one.

Country X borders yours, but speaks another language, has different product-labeling rules and lower incomes. Country Y is a two-day ship away, but shares your language, belongs to the same trade agreement and has similar incomes. Which do you choose?

options.text: Country X. Trucks get there in a day.
options.feedback: Cheap, fast delivery is real. But you'd relabel every product, learn new rules and reprice for smaller budgets, and those costs never stop.

options.text: Country Y. Shared language, rules and incomes.
options.feedback: You pay more for shipping, but your products, prices and store playbook work almost as they are. Most of what makes a market hard isn't the miles.

options.text: Whichever country has the most people
options.feedback: A big market is only worth what you can capture. If it's far from you in every other way, its size mostly measures how much you could lose.

cards.title: The short drive came with a long list.
body: Picture the chain that picks Country X. The trucks are cheap. Everything else is not.

Every package needs new labels. Some products fail local safety rules and must be sourced again. The bestsellers at home sit on shelves because they're priced for richer shoppers. The ads don't land, because the jokes don't translate.
None of these costs appeared on the map. All of them showed up in the profit and loss.

cards.title: Distance between markets has four parts.
body: **Distance between markets** is how different two places are in the ways that matter to your business. In a 2001 Harvard Business Review essay, strategist Pankaj Ghemawat split it into four kinds. A country can be close on one and far on the others.

breakdown.label: How rules work
breakdown.detail: Laws, tariffs, standards, currency, trade deals

breakdown.label: How far things travel
breakdown.detail: Miles, time zones, ports, roads, climate

cards.callout: Add up all four, not just the miles.
cards.softwareNote: For software, geographic distance nearly vanishes, but the other three stay. Data and privacy rules, local payment methods, language and what people can afford still decide whether an app travels.

cards.title: Trade follows more than the miles.
body: Economists who study trade use what they call a *gravity model*. Countries trade more when their economies are bigger and less when they're farther apart, like gravity between planets.
But the same research finds that other things matter as much as kilometers. Countries trade more when they share a language, a border, a trade agreement or a currency, or have old historical ties.
Ghemawat's point was simple: if trade bends around these differences, so will your sales.

image.label: Two countries linked by four lines of different thickness
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 두 개의 추상적인 나라 모양을 네 개의 선(문화, 제도, 지리, 경제)이 잇고, 선마다 굵기가 달라 가까움과 멂을 표현. 실제 국가 모양이나 국기는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which distance hurts depends on what you sell.
body: The four kinds don't weigh the same for every business. Ask which one your product is most sensitive to.
list: **Heavy or perishable goods** (cement, fresh food): geographic distance
**Regulated goods** (medicine, food, electrical parts): administrative distance
**Products tied to taste** (snacks, fashion, media): cultural distance
**Products tied to income** (premium brands, durable goods): economic distance
cards.callout: The same pair of countries can be close for one business and far for another.

cards.title: Distance is a cost, not a verdict.
body: Sometimes distance is the reason to go. A big gap in labor costs or prices is economic distance, and many factories move abroad to use exactly that.
Distance also shifts. Trade deals, tariffs and exchange rates can move a country closer or farther within a few years.
So measure distance to price the effort and plan for it, not to rule markets in or out on instinct.

image.label: A dial labeled distance with arrows moving both ways
image.brief: 단순한 3D 클레이 스타일. '거리' 다이얼이 가운데 있고, 한쪽에는 비용 표시(동전이 빠져나감), 다른 쪽에는 기회 표시(동전이 들어옴). 영어 라벨 "Cost"와 "Opportunity".

cards.title: Now it's a steel-shelving factory.
body: You make heavy, low-priced steel shelving for warehouses. Two importers want your product.
One is across the sea and shares your language. The other is a day's drive away, but charges a tariff on steel goods and requires its own safety certification. What should you work out first?

options.text: Go with the importer who shares your language
options.feedback: Easier calls and paperwork help. But for a heavy, cheap product, the language gap is rarely what decides your margin.

options.text: Compare the full landed cost per unit: freight, tariff and certification
options.feedback: Your product is most sensitive to geographic and administrative distance. Putting both into one number per unit shows which market actually leaves you money.

options.text: Pick the richer country, since buyers can pay more
options.feedback: Warehouse shelving is bought on price, not prestige. Higher incomes won't cover sea freight on steel if the cost per unit is too high.

cards.title: Measure distance in four ways, not in miles.
body: Before choosing a new market, ask how far it is in culture, rules, geography and economics, and which of those your product feels most.
**Try it today:** pick one country you've considered selling to. Rate it close, medium or far on each of the four kinds of distance. Circle the one that would cost you most.
